title: EGY-07 · The possession, the family and the house

blocks.text: EGY-07 · The possession, the family and the house
Lesson overview

In Egypt the family is the first topic of conversation: who are you, who are yours, where they live, how many children they have. In this unit you learn to say "My, your, your" in Egyptian, with the suffixes (bitna "our house," ʾōḍti My room is with the word bitāʿ , typical of dialect (il-mobāyl bitāʿi My cell phone (s); kinship names, with the distinction between ʿamm and ḫāl that the Italian does not do; The vocabulary of the house and the apartment. Six weeks, in parallel with B1-17, B1-18 and B1-19.

rows: 8–9 hours · six weeks (weeks 131–136), about 1,5 hours per week in two blocks

blocks.text: Materials This unit, a tutor or Egyptian conversation partner, some photos (also taken from the web) for oral production
Targets. At the end of the unit you know:
1. use possessive suffixes with names, even those in -a (ʾōḍa → ʾōḍti) and with aḫḫ (abūya, aḫūya);
2. use bitāʿ, bitāʿit, bitūʿ and ask who it is?bitāʿ mīn?);
3. present a family with Egyptian kinship names;
4. describe a house or apartment: rooms, furniture, floor, rent;
5. distinguish ʿandi "ho" is the name of the manufacturer. maʿāya I have with me and bitāʿi It's mine.
Six-week plan (two blocks from 40–45 minutes per week).

What to notice. Possession with the suffixes: bitna is our home ʾōḍti My room is mamtak your mother, ḫāli "My uncle" mirātu His wife, wladhum, their children, with bitāʿ: il-balakōna btaʿitna Our balcony is located in the heart of the city. btāʿit mīn? "Who's"? ʾōḍit Yāsmīn The chamber of YāsmīnIn front of a complement the -a becomes -it (like the tāʾ marbūṭa in fuṣḥā). ṭanṭ "Zia" is an affectionate title for family ladies or family friends. tēta "Grandma" is a song by American singer-songwriter and singer-songwriter. kullina "all of us." baʿatithāli "Me sent them" (baʿat + en + ha + li).
2. The possession in Egyptian and in fuṣḥā
As in fuṣḥā, possession is expressed by the suffixes on the name. Plus, the Egyptian has bitāʿ , a word that means "di," belonging to "di" and which is put after the name with the article.
3. The possessive suffixes
Three rules.
1. The names in -a take -it- (or -t-) before the suffix: šaʾʾa → šaʾʾiti, šaʾʾitak; ʿarabiyya → ʿarabiyyiti; ʾōḍa → ʾōḍti,
ʾoḍitha.
2. The long vowel shortens before two consonants: bēt + na → bitna, ʾōḍit + ha→ ʾoḍitha. In front of a suffix beginning with vowel remains long: bētak, bētu.
3. abb and aḫḫ have special shapes with -ū-: abūya, abūk, abūh; aḫūya, aḫūk, aḫūha. Without suffix, in front of a name: abu Šarīf, aḫu māma.
4. bitāʿ
Forms. bitāʿ agree with the possession, not the owner.
+ inta bitāʿak bitaʿtak bitūʿak
+ iḥna bitaʿna bitaʿitna bituʿna

Examples: il-mobāyl bitāʿi My cell phone is in the middle of it. iš-šanṭa btaʿti My purse is actually okub bitūʿi My books. After a word that ends in vowel the initial i falls: il-ʿarabiyya btaʿtak. When to use bitāʿ.
1. With foreign words and long words, where the suffix sounds strange: the-laptop bitāʿi, il-asansēr bitāʿ on-
ʿimāra.
2. To highlight or contrast: from miš bitāʿi, from bitāʿak! It's not mine, it's yours!
3. To ask who it is: bitāʿ mīn? · btāʿit mīn? · btūʿ mīn?
4. Never with kinship names: ummi, aḫūya, mirāti, not ... bitaʿti».

With many common names the two forms are possible: kitābi = il-kitāb bitāʿi. In conversation bitāʿ is more frequent; in the curated writing and in the affective words one prefers the suffix. Other uses of bitāʿ. bitāʿ + name also indicates the name of... bitāʿ il-fūl The seller of fūl»; bitāʿ ʿašara ginēh From about ten pounds.
5. Family

rows: Uncle Aunt (brother and sister of the father)
Uncle Aunt (brother and sister of the mother)
my cousin (son of my father's uncle) · my cousin (daughter of the mother's aunt)

blocks.text: ⁧قرايب⁩ ʾarāyib The cousin doesn't exist. Arabic does not have a word for "cousin": it is said of whom he is a son. ibn ʿammi, ibn ḫāli, ibn ʿammiti, ibn ḫālti They're four different people. mirāt "Wife" is used with a complement: mirāti, mirāt Ḥusām. For the sake of the lady alone, it is said that she is-sitt or madām. il-ḥagga is a respectful way to talk about your wife or an elderly lady (Lett. "He who made the pilgrimage").

9. Pronunciation

The vowels that shorten. bēt/bitna, ʾōḍa/ʾoḍitha, bitāʿ/bitaʿha: Listen to the tutor and repeat the couples. It's the same rule you feel in kitābak/kitabha. abūya, aḫūya. The ū is long and accented: a-BŪ-ya, a-ḪŪ-ya. Don't say "abuya" fast. ʿamm and ḫāl. The ʿ of ʿamm and the ḫ of ḫāl separate two different persons: trained with ʿammi / ḫāli, ʿammiti / ḫālti.
